name: Chiropractic BioPhysics (CBP) cervical lordosis
lead: Chiropractic BioPhysics (CBP) is a posture-focused chiropractic technique founded in December 1980 by Donald Harrison, Deanne Harrison and Daniel Murphy. It uses a mathematical model of ideal spinal curves and combines adjustments, exercises and traction to restore them.[1] Cervical lordosis, the natural forward curve of the neck, is one of its main targets.

For appearance, the interest is in neck and head posture. A restored curve is meant to bring the head back over the shoulders and reduce the forward-head, rounded-shoulder look, giving a straighter profile, a longer-looking neck and a more upright stance. Forward head posture is described on Wikipedia as the head sitting ahead of the shoulders, with the ear lobe in front of a vertical line through the shoulder point, and it is paired with rounded shoulders in what is called upper crossed syndrome.[2]

CBP is built around measured treatment: practitioners take X-rays, compare the patient's curves with the Harrison Spinal Model, and then apply a mirror-image program of positioning, exercises, adjustments and sustained extension traction, including foam orthotics such as the Denneroll that are also used at home.[1]

Proponents also claim that restoring the curve reduces pain and improves function. A 2005 review of CBP publications, written within the chiropractic field, rated CBP evidence as comparable to spinal manipulation for neck pain,[3] and a 2017 randomized trial reported that adding Denneroll extension traction to a multimodal program increased cervical lordosis in patients.[4] Grokipedia notes that critics question whether curve deviations relate to symptoms and point to the affiliation of many study authors with CBP.[1]

paras: CBP uses the Harrison Spinal Model, a geometric model of ideal sagittal alignment traced along the posterior vertebral bodies. The cervical curve is modelled as a circular arc, while thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis are modelled as elliptical shapes, and the model serves as the main treatment goal.[1] Grokipedia cites radiograph measurements with mean cervical angles of about 34.5 degrees in asymptomatic people, 28.6 in acute neck pain and 22.0 in chronic neck pain as validation for the model.[1]

The signature Mirror Image approach positions the patient opposite their abnormal posture before adjustments, exercises or traction, and corrections aim at roughly twice the measured displacement to overcome soft-tissue resistance. The structural rehabilitation protocol, summarised as exercises, adjustments and traction (E.A.T.), places exercises first, then drop-table, instrument or manual adjustments, then traction.[1]

Sustained extension traction lasts 10 to 20 minutes per session using cervical, thoracic, lumbar or three-point bending set-ups. The Denneroll is a high-density foam orthotic in cervical, thoracic and lumbar versions, used in clinic and at home; cervical placements include C7-T2, C4-C6 and C2-C4.[1]

A relief phase of about 12 visits over three weeks is followed by structural rehabilitation of 30 to 40 sessions over 9 to 12 weeks at three to five visits per week, with home support introduced around week 8 and re-evaluations about every 36 visits or 12 weeks.[1]

Donald Harrison originated the Mirror Image postural methods in March 1980, shortly before CBP was formally founded in December 1980. He earned his chiropractic degree in 1979 and holds degrees in mathematics and mechanical engineering, including a PhD in applied mathematics (1998).[1] Between 1980 and 1986 Donald Harrison and Glenn Harrison developed Mirror Image exercises and traction methods, and CBP Non-Profit, Inc. was founded in 1982 to support research. From 1996 to 2000 Deed Harrison, now CEO, refined cervical traction and developed thoracic and lumbar traction methods.[1] Grokipedia also records that Harrison criticised the scientific rigour of the Pettibon method after working with it in the late 1970s.[1]

Forward head posture places the head forward of the shoulders and is often paired with rounded shoulders; it is associated in the literature with phone and computer use, and with occupations that involve sustained bent postures such as dentistry, hairdressing, nursing and teaching.[2] Wikipedia lists neck and upper-trapezius pain, cervicogenic headache and joint locking among associated problems, and a 2019 systematic review it cites found a link between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not adolescents.[2]

A review of the literature found cervical lordosis values to be significantly associated with thoracic kyphosis values, and rounded shoulders with increased thoracic kyphosis.[5] CBP treats the neck curve as part of a whole-spine model, so its programs also address head translation and upper-back posture.[1] Other approaches to head posture listed on Wikipedia include strengthening deep neck flexors and shoulder-blade retractors, stretching the upper trapezius, ergonomic changes, yoga and Pilates.[2]

CBP certification is a voluntary post-graduate program run by CBP Seminars, Inc.: general certification takes seven seminars (about 90 hours), a written exam, X-ray analysis and a practical demonstration, and advanced certification adds seven more seminars (about 180 hours total) and a case presentation. No state mandates CBP; chiropractic licensing is state-level.[1]

A 2005 review of Clinical Biomechanics of Posture publications, the earlier name for CBP, compared controlled trials of CBP and spinal manipulation; it rated CBP evidence as roughly equal to spinal manipulation for neck pain and above the diversified technique taught in chiropractic colleges, and proposed a structural rehabilitation protocol [3].

A 2017 randomized controlled trial in 72 patients aged 40 to 55 with cervicogenic dizziness, a hypolordotic neck and anterior head translation compared a multimodal program with the same program plus Denneroll cervical traction; the traction group showed greater improvement in cervical lordosis, pain, head repositioning accuracy and dizziness outcomes at ten weeks and at one-year follow-up [4].

According to Grokipedia, a lateral X-ray study reported mean cervical angles of about 34.5 degrees in asymptomatic people, 28.6 in acute neck pain and 22.0 in chronic neck pain, and a non-randomized trial reported a 13.6 degree gain in C2-C7 Cobb angle with about 70 percent retention at 14 months [1]. Critics noted in the same source observe that curve deviations occur in many people without symptoms and that many trials are non-randomized and CBP-affiliated [1].

Grokipedia counts 381 peer-reviewed CBP items across 63 journals, including 21 randomized controlled trials, 7 non-randomized controlled trials, 7 prospective cohorts, 178 case reports or series and 15 systematic reviews, and describes CBP as among the most published named chiropractic techniques.[1] The same source reports a non-randomized cervical trial in which treated patients averaged 38 visits over 14.6 weeks and gained 13.6 degrees in C2-C7 Cobb angle, with anterior head translation falling by 11 mm, pain on a 0-10 scale dropping from 4.1 to 1.1, and about 70 percent keeping the gain at 14 months while controls showed no significant change.[1] It also reports a systematic review of three lumbar trials with lordosis gains of 6.2 to 11.3 degrees.[1]

A rapid review cited by Grokipedia found no good evidence that routine spinal X-rays improve outcomes, raising radiation exposure questions, since CBP uses radiographs to measure curves.[1] Critics cited there also note weak links between sagittal curves and pain, mixed treatments that obscure CBP-specific effects, and heavy affiliation of authors with CBP organisations.[1]

Spinal manipulation in general has mild to moderate temporary effects such as local discomfort, headache and tiredness; rare serious outcomes include vertebral artery dissection and stroke, and whether cervical manipulation is causal is disputed. Wikipedia reports that there is not enough data to establish the overall rate of adverse events.[6]

card.summary: Chiropractic traction and exercise system aiming to restore the neck curve; evidence is mostly from CBP-affiliated studies.
card.note: Relies on spinal X-rays; evidence mostly from affiliated authors.

quick.overview:
CBP is a chiropractic system that tries to restore the neck's forward curve (cervical lordosis) using traction, exercises and adjustments.

Most supporting studies come from CBP-affiliated authors, and critics question whether curve changes relate to symptoms.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners measure curves on X-rays and apply sustained extension traction, orthotics and Mirror Image positioning intended to produce lasting tissue change.
quick.risks: Repeated X-rays add radiation exposure, and neck manipulation has been associated with rare stroke. Certification is voluntary.

chain: Head carried further back over the shoulders
angle.text: CBP practitioners aim to reshape the neck curve so the head sits over the shoulders instead of forward of them. People seeking a more upright posture, a more defined neck line and a less forward-jutting chin use it for that outcome.
